ad2_what_holds.topic: Where the taught American Dream holds: income levels, mobility of immigrants' children, place, Black and Hispanic gains, GI Bill era, goods

claims.text: Chetty et al. (Science 2017): share of children earning more than their parents (absolute mobility) about 90% for the 1940 birth cohort, about 50% for children born in the 1980s; decline robust to alternative price deflators, income definitions and tax/transfer adjustments; higher GDP growth alone would not restore it; 1940-cohort distribution of growth would reverse more than 70% of the decline

Opportunity Insights summary: sons vs fathers' earnings 95% (1940) and 41% (1984 cohort); absolute mobility fell in all 50 states, most in industrial Midwest (Michigan, Illinois); 1940s-50s GDP growth with today's distribution raises mobility only to 62%; today's GDP distributed as in the 1940s raises it to 80%

Abramitzky et al. (AER 2021): using millions of father-son pairs over more than 100 years, children of immigrants from nearly every sending country have higher upward mobility than children of US-born parents, historically and today; part of the advantage comes from immigrant families locating in places with better opportunities

Abramitzky et al. (NBER WP): sons of immigrant fathers at the 25th percentile reached ranks 3-4 percentiles above sons of US-born fathers (1880-1910); about 5 percentile points in modern data (Opportunity Insights and GSS); exceptions in modern data include Haiti and Jamaica

Chetty, Dobbie, Goldman, Porter, Yang (2024): between the 1978 and 1992 birth cohorts Black children's earnings rose at all parental income levels; white-Black earnings gaps for children from low-income families fell 30%; class gaps among white children widened 30%; same pattern for education, test scores, mortality

Chetty, Hendren, Jones, Porter: 'Hispanic Americans are moving up significantly in the income distribution across generations' with relatively high intergenerational mobility; Black Americans have substantially lower upward mobility than whites

Chetty, Hendren, Kline, Saez (QJE 2014): probability that a child raised in the bottom fifth reaches the top fifth about 4.4% in Charlotte vs 12.9% in San Jose; higher mobility areas have less residential segregation, less income inequality, better primary schools, more social capital, more family stability; data on 40m+ children

VA: Roosevelt signed the GI Bill 22 June 1944; veterans were 49% of college admissions in 1947; by 25 July 1956, 7.8 million of 16 million WWII veterans had used education or training benefits; VA backed nearly 2.4 million home loans 1944-1952

Turner and Bound: WWII service plus GI Bill raised college attainment about 0.4 years for Black men born outside the South and about 0.3 years for white men, but Southern-born Black veterans saw few gains; the bill 'exacerbated rather than narrowed' Black-white gaps among Southern men; about 100 institutions open to Black students in the South

USDA ERS (2026): Americans spent 9.7% of disposable personal income on food in 2025 (4.8% at home, 4.9% away) vs 10.4% in 1997; in 2024 the lowest income quintile spent 33.0% of before-tax income on food vs 6.4% for the highest
USDA ERS (2020 chart): total food took 17.0% of disposable personal income in 1960 and 9.5% in 2019
Census C25: share of new one-family houses completed with air-conditioning 49% (1973), 63% (1980), 76% (1990), 85% (2000), 89% (2008)

OECD Society at a Glance 2024 Fig 4.1 (via Wikipedia table): median equivalised household disposable income 2021, USD PPP: Luxembourg 49,748, United States 46,625 (2nd), Norway 41,621, Switzerland 39,698, Canada 39,388
OECD Better Life Index: in the United States the top 20% of the population earn about eight times as much as the bottom 20%

ad2_how_to_measure.topic: How to measure the Dream: absolute vs relative mobility, income vs wealth, median vs mean, real vs nominal, household vs individual, price index

claims.text: Chetty et al. (2014): percentile rank-based intergenerational mobility 'extremely stable' for the 1971-1993 birth cohorts; probability of moving from bottom fifth to top fifth 8.4% (1971 cohort) and 9.0% (1986 cohort); 'the rungs of the ladder have grown further apart'; consequences of the 'birth lottery' larger today than in the past
NBER Digest: college attendance gap between highest- and lowest-income children 74.5 points (1984 cohort) and 69.2 points (1993 cohort); mobility fairly stable in each of nine census divisions

SCF 2025 Table 1 (2024 income, 2025 dollars): median family income $82.2k, mean $145.2k; median by race: White non-Hispanic $95.3k, Black non-Hispanic $49.4k, Hispanic $66.8k. Table 2: median net worth all $215.9k, mean $1,241.5k; White $332.1k, Black $36.8k, Hispanic $79.6k. Report gives standard errors for subgroups only online

Census uses the chained CPI-U (C-CPI-U) to adjust income from 2000 onward (adopted 2023 after an interagency working group recommendation) and the R-CPI-U-RS and earlier series before 2000; median household income 2023 $80,610 nominal = $82,690 in 2024 dollars; C-CPI-U prices +2.6% 2023-24
Census (Dec 2025): 39.7 million one-person households in 2025, 29% of households, up from 20% in 1975

Reeves and Halikias (Brookings 2017), summarising Scott Winship: adjusting for smaller family size raises the share of 1980s-born children better off than parents from 50% to 60%; replicating in PSID and switching from CPI-U-RS to the PCE deflator raises it to 67%; including transfer income to 68%

BLS: the C-CPI-U uses a superlative formula to account for consumers substituting across item categories, with weights varying monthly; the CPI-U assumes no substitution across categories and updates weights annually; C-CPI-U published from July 2002 data; December-to-December difference averaged about 0.2 percentage points lower, 2001-2023, though occasionally higher

BEA: CPI and PCE price index differ by formula (PCE Fisher-Ideal vs CPI modified Laspeyres), weights and scope: PCE covers 'spending by and on behalf of the personal sector', CPI 'out-of-pocket spending by households'
